Article Title: China rejects Anthropic allegations of using Claude to train their models
Article Text:
China rejects Anthropic's AI extraction allegations

What Anthropic’s report alleges

Moonshot, DeepSeek accused of similar tactics

China has firmly rejected accusations by US artificial intelligence company Anthropic that Chinese AI labs, including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI, carried out large-scale efforts to extract responses from its Claude models and use them to train their own systems.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing “advocates AI for good” and accused Anthropic of “distorting facts”.“We firmly oppose attempts to throw mud at China by distorting facts,” Mao said at a regular news conference on Friday.The comments came a day after Anthropic released a threat intelligence report alleging that several China-based AI companies had conducted what it called “illicit distillation” campaigns against Claude.Distillation is a common AI training technique in which a less powerful model learns from the outputs of a more capable model. Anthropic alleged that Chinese AI labs went further by using networks of accounts to systematically send prompts to Claude, collect its responses and use those exchanges to improve their own models.According to the report, the operations involved more than 151 million exchanges with Claude by Alibaba alone between May and July, making it the largest distillation campaign Anthropic said it had measured.The activity peaked at nearly 3 million exchanges a day and involved more than 3,500 accounts that Anthropic described as fraudulent. The company said Alibaba used Claude’s outputs to train its Qwen models and also used the model for wider AI research, including reinforcement learning and model architecture work.Anthropic said some of the exchanges involved sensitive information belonging to individual users, multinational companies and state-affiliated organisations. It said such practices were likely inconsistent with privacy laws and the companies’ own terms of service.Anthropic also accused Beijing-based Moonshot AI of secretly routing Kimi users’ requests to Claude and using some exchanges to train its models. The company said Moonshot relayed nearly 300,000 requests through 5,380 accounts in 10 days and more than 23 million exchanges between May and July. DeepSeek was accused of similar tactics, with Anthropic reporting more than 12 million distillation attacks over 14 days in July. Xiaomi was also named in the report.Anthropic said some unauthorised exchanges exposed sensitive data, including internal CCTV footage from Chengdu. It said it detected and disrupted the alleged operations between December 2025 and August 2026 across seven areas of AI misuse, including cyber operations, surveillance, fraud, weapons development and model distillation.
Article Summary: China rejects anthropic's ai extraction allegations. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson mao ning said beijing ‘advocates ai for good’ and accused anthropic of ‘distorting facts’ us artificial intelligence company anthropic alleged that chinese ai labs carried out large-scale efforts to extract responses from its claude models.

Article Title: In 1900, North American tall goldenrod was introduced to Japan for gardens and honey production, but it escaped cultivation and overran native grasslands nationwide
Article Text:
A bee feeds on the flowers of tall goldenrod (Solidago altissima) in Pittsburgh's Beechview neighbourhood. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A plant that flourished precisely where no one wanted it

Choking out the grasses that get in first

Tall goldenrod (Solidago altissima) growing in a dense stand. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A plant still adapting to Japan

The majority of plants brought in for beekeeping and gardening remain exactly where they are planted; thus, they rarely receive any attention. Occasionally, however, a species that appears innocuous in a flower bed has very different ambitions when it comes to open space. One of the most obvious instances of that pattern in the world is the tall, late-blooming perennial tall goldenrod, which is native to North America. Japan has been observing the effects of this pattern throughout its countryside for more than a century.Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies records the first introduction of tall goldenrod at around 1900, when it was deliberately brought in as an ornamental plant and nectar source. It was intentionally introduced as an ornamental garden plant and a nectar source for honeybees because it blooms unusually late in the year, from October through December in much of Japan, when few other plants are still flowering.In its first several decades in Japan, tall goldenrod did much of what gardeners expected of it, staying mainly limited to the plots where it was planted. This changed abruptly in the years after the Second World War, when the plant grew swiftly throughout the country, going well out of gardens into riverbanks, vacant lots, the boundaries of farmland and roadsides.Today, it is established across almost the entire Japanese archipelago.Its success is partly a matter of raw biology. According to the CABI Compendium , tall goldenrod is an international scientific reference maintained by the nonprofit research organisation CABI. Tall goldenrod produces huge numbers of wind-dispersed seeds and also spreads aggressively through underground rhizomes, allowing a single colonising plant to expand into a dense stand within a few growing seasons. It also exudes allelopathic molecules from its roots, chemicals that restrict the germination and growth of competing plants nearby. This gives tall goldenrod an edge over the natural flora in the same patch of soil. Studies comparing Japanese populations with those in the native range have found that the invasive plants tend to grow taller, produce more leaves and release higher concentrations of suppressive compounds, suggesting they have become more aggressive since arriving in Japan.Japan’s natural grassland populations have mostly borne the ecological penalty. Once established, tall goldenrod forms dense stands that crowd out native grasses and wildflowers that would otherwise share the open ground. The National Institute for Environmental Studies mentions competition with native species and allelopathic suppression as the two known effects of the plant, with native grasses specifically identified among the affected plant. The institute classifies tall goldenrod as one of the 100 worst invasive alien species in Japan, a list of introduced organisms that are considered to cause substantial and enduring damage to the country’s ecosystems.Tall goldenrod remains widespread in Japan, despite its classification as one of the country's 100 worst invasive alien species. NIES lists competition with native species and allelopathic effects among its impacts and notes that pulling and repeated mowing can be used to control established plants. Part of the rationale comes from the very stuff that made the plant desirable in the first place. Its late-season blooms continue to provide a key source of nectar for honeybees and other pollinating insects as they enter the winter months, and wholesale removal from a landscape can leave those insects with fewer options at a time of year when alternatives are already few. They have a dilemma, an unwelcome invader battling a plant that some elements of the ecology and the beekeeping industry have discreetly grown to depend on.Scientists examining tall goldenrod in Japan have revealed that the populations there are not just frozen copies of those in North America. A reciprocal transplant study summarised by the National Center for Biotechnology Information found evolutionary differences between the two regions, including changes in the resistance of Japanese populations to local insect pests compared with plants in their native range. For example, a species of lace bug that arrived in Japan from the United States fairly recently reacts differently to the goldenrod's resistance mechanisms there than it does to the same plant species back home, a sign that a century and a quarter of separation has already started to alter the way the species defends itself. More than a century after tall goldenrod was brought to a few Japanese gardens for its late flowers and its value to bees, it is one of the most obvious examples in the country of how a plant chosen for one thing can do something else altogether when left to its own devices in unfamiliar soil.
Article Summary: Tall goldenrod (solidago altissima) is native to north america. It was introduced to japan in 1900 as an ornamental plant and a nectar source for honeybees because it blooms unusually late in the year. Once established, tall goldenrod forms dense stands that crowd out native grasses and wildflowers that would otherwise share the open ground.

Article Title: A 26-year-old Canadian hacker breached 165 companies and exposed data linked to 100 million people, but an investigation eventually led to his guilty plea
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How the hacking operation began and exposed billions of records

What was taken from the companies

PC: AI Generated

The stolen data became a source of ransom demands

How the stolen data became another source of profit

How investigators closed in on the Canadian suspect

What charges does Moucka face after pleading guilty

The case forms part of a wider FBI operation

A hacking operation that began in early 2024 reached far beyond the companies directly targeted. A 26-year-old Canadian man, Connor Riley Moucka of Kitchener, Ontario, has admitted taking part in a campaign that compromised data held by at least 165 customers of a US-based software company. The stolen material ran into billions of records and several terabytes of information, according to US court documents. It included financial details, payroll information, identity documents and records relating to calls and text messages. The attackers then demanded money from victims, while some of the stolen data was also offered for sale online. Moucka pleaded guilty in August 2026 and is due to be sentenced in October.The conspiracy operated between February and October 2024, according to prosecutors. Moucka and his associates obtained login credentials that allowed them to get into cloud-hosted information belonging to customers of a US software-as-a-service provider.Once inside, they were able to access the computer systems of individual customer organisations. The scale of the material taken was substantial. Investigators say the group downloaded terabytes of information and obtained billions of sensitive customer records across the affected organisations.The victims were not limited to one particular type of business. The stolen information reflected the different kinds of data held by the companies using the cloud service, which meant that the attackers gained access to records belonging to ordinary customers as well as information used internally by organisations.Among the information obtained were non-content records showing individuals' call and text histories. The hackers also accessed banking and other financial information, payroll records and registration numbers associated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration.Personal identity information was part of the haul too. Driver's licence numbers, passport numbers, Social Security numbers and other personally identifiable information were among the records taken during the breaches.According to The US Department of Justice, the consequences extended to at least 100 million people whose information was held by the affected companies. That figure refers to customers connected to the victim organisations and does not mean that every individual had every type of personal record exposed.After obtaining the information, the conspirators began putting pressure on victims. They threatened to release stolen data publicly unless money was paid.The operation generated more than $2.5 million in ransom payments, according to prosecutors. Moucka himself received at least $495,000 from the wider scheme, as reported.In one case, the pressure did not stop after an initial extortion attempt. Moucka allegedly used previously stolen information to demand further payment from a victim, threatening another disclosure of data. The information used in that attempt included material belonging to a government officer and members of the immediate family of a former government officer.That second demand showed how stolen information could continue to be used against a victim after the original breach had taken place.Extortion was not the only way the group sought to make money from the stolen records.Prosecutors said the conspirators advertised data belonging to victims for sale on several cybercrime forums and through Telegram. The marketplaces named in the case included BreachForums, Exploit.in and XSS.is.The stolen information therefore had a potential value beyond the ransom demands made directly to companies. Data taken during the attacks could be offered to other people involved in cybercrime, creating another route for the information to circulate.According to the US Department of Justice, the financial damage recorded by investigators was considerably larger than Moucka's personal proceeds. Victim companies suffered more than $9.5 million in actual losses, according to the Justice Department. That calculation does not include the losses experienced by the companies' customers.The hacking campaign did not continue indefinitely. Moucka was arrested in Canada after the investigation brought international law enforcement agencies into the case.The Justice Department's Office of International Affairs helped secure his arrest and his extradition to the United States in July 2025. The FBI worked with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and several other foreign agencies during the investigation.Authorities from Australia, Spain, Ukraine and Turkey also assisted. Their involvement reflected the international nature of an investigation in which a Canadian suspect allegedly targeted organisations and customers in multiple jurisdictions.By the time Moucka entered his guilty plea on August 5, 2026, the case had been under investigation for nearly two years.Moucka pleaded guilty to four counts in the indictment. They include computer fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and a related conspiracy charge.The aggravated identity theft count carries a mandatory minimum sentence of two years in prison. The other charges carry maximum penalties of up to 30 years, although the final sentence will depend on the court's assessment of the case, the federal sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. Moucka is scheduled to be sentenced on October 27.His guilty plea resolves his criminal responsibility for the charges to which he admitted, but the full financial and personal impact of the breaches reaches well beyond the defendant himself. Companies recorded millions of dollars in losses, while information connected to at least 100 million people was caught up in the wider data theft.The investigation was carried out by the FBI as part of Operation Riptide, an enforcement campaign aimed at cybercriminal networks, their infrastructure and the financial systems used to support cyber-enabled crime and fraud.The Justice Department's Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section prosecuted the case alongside the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington. International agencies played a role in locating and arresting Moucka and bringing him to the United States.The case also sits within a broader increase in reported cybercrime losses in the US. The FBI said Americans reported more than $20 billion in cybercrime losses during the previous year, representing a 26% increase in a single year.For Moucka, the next stage is sentencing. For the organisations caught up in the 2024 breaches, the consequences began much earlier, when credentials were used to gain access to cloud-hosted systems and vast amounts of customer information were taken.
Article Summary: Connor riley moucka of kitchener, ontario, admitted taking part in a campaign that compromised data held by at least 165 customers of a us-based software company. The stolen material ran into billions of records and several terabytes of information. It included financial details, payroll information, identity documents and records relating to calls and text messages.

Article Title: Meet Meera Ramaswami: The Ann Arbor inventor who turned her grandmother’s fall into a patented mobility device and launched a company
Article Text:
Meera Ramaswami, Founder at CargilityPhoto: Meera Ramaswami/ LinkedIn

A familiar moment with serious consequences

How the device works

Recognition through The Henry Ford

From invention to patent

A mother and daughter become co-founders

The wider need for mobility support

Building an Ann Arbor company

A personal problem becomes a public solution

A fall while getting out of a car changed the direction of Meera Ramaswami’s life. She watched her grandmother lose her balance during a moment that should have been routine, then saw the injury heal while the fear remained. Her grandmother became less willing to travel, and Meera began thinking about how a small loss of stability could lead to isolation and lost independence. That question eventually became Cargility, an Ann Arbor company developing a portable mobility aid that helps people enter and exit vehicles safely. Meera designed the device, tested prototypes, earned recognition through The Henry Ford’s Invention Convention and secured a US utility patent. As reported by The Henry Ford and Ann Arbor SPARK, the invention has grown from a family experience into a company founded by Meera and her mother, Praveena Ramaswami.Getting into or out of a car is an ordinary action for most people, but it can become difficult after an injury, during ageing or for anyone with balance and mobility challenges. A person may need to twist, lower themselves, find a stable surface and stand on uneven ground, all while managing the distance between the seat and pavement.For Meera’s grandmother, that moment led to a fall. The physical injury eventually healed, but the emotional effect lasted longer. Fear of falling again changed how willing she was to leave home. A simple vehicle transfer became a barrier to travel, social connection and independence.Meera recognised that the problem was larger than one family. Older adults, people recovering from surgery or rehabilitation, people with disabilities and caregivers may all face difficulties during vehicle entry and exit. Existing solutions such as walking frames, canes or assistance from another person may not be convenient in the narrow space beside a car. Observation to design Meera began developing the concept in 2022, using a process of observation, prototyping and testing. She didn’t start with an abstract engineering problem, but rather looked at a specific moment in everyday life and asked what kind of support would make it safer. The device needed to be portable, strong and compatible with different passenger vehicles. It also had to be easy enough for a user or caregiver to position without complicated installation. A support that worked only in one type of car would have limited value, so adaptability became an important part of the design.The resulting product, Cargility, is a door to floor mobility assistive device. It engages with the striker in a vehicle’s doorframe and creates a stable support point. An articulating leg reaches the ground, allowing the user to lean on a railing while entering or exiting the vehicle.The design is intended to reduce fall risk and ease the physical strain placed on caregivers. It provides a fixed point of support during the transfer rather than requiring a person to rely on a moving car door or another individual’s strength.The Cargility tool is designed to connect with the striker plate, the metal component in the vehicle doorframe that receives the door latch. Once engaged, the device holds a stable relationship to the vehicle. Its articulating leg consists of two members connected by a pivot, so that the structure can accommodate various vehicle heights and configurations. When positioned correctly, the leg reaches the ground and supports a handrail or bar that the user can hold.The aim is to create a continuous point of stability between the vehicle and the ground. A person can use the rail while lowering into the seat or standing up, reducing the need to twist quickly or search for something to grip.The tool is not intended to replace a doctor, physical therapist or properly prescribed mobility aid. Its purpose is to make one specific part of everyday movement safer and more manageable. The device would still need to be attached correctly and users need to follow the instructions before they can rely on it. Testing and refining the inventionDeveloping the first concept was only the beginning. Meera tested different designs and compared their performance. Earlier descriptions of her work indicate that she created possible models, evaluated them and selected the design that performed best.This kind of testing is central to invention education. A promising idea may fail when exposed to weight, movement, different surfaces or different vehicle shapes.Prototypes expose weaknesses that aren’t apparent on paper. Meera’s work also involved a balancing act between conflicting requirements. The device had to be strong enough to hold a person, but portable enough to carry. It had to fit different cars, but be stable. It had to be easy for users, but not compromise safety. The process required engineering knowledge, but also empathy.A technically impressive device would not be useful if older adults or caregivers found it too complicated. Designing for real people meant considering reach, grip, balance, strength and confidence.Meera’s invention gained recognition through the Invention Convention, a programme supported by The Henry Ford that encourages young people to identify problems and develop solutions. The programme teaches students to move through stages including constructing a prototype, testing it, revising the design and communicating the final idea.In 2022, Meera received top honours in four engineering categories at the Invention Convention held at the Henry Ford Museum.Those awards included innovation, safety, Make the World and the Grand Prize, which provided support for bringing the invention to the US Patent Office.The recognition helped Meera to validate the invention and gain access to a network of mentors, educators and organizations experienced in product development. It also helped turn the project from a student design into an innovation with commercial potential.For young inventors, programmes like the Invention Convention can provide something that classrooms often cannot. They offer a structured way to develop an idea, receive feedback and present it to people who understand engineering and entrepreneurship.Cargility’s mobility concept eventually became a patented technology.Meera Ramaswami was awarded the US patent “Vehicle Access Mobility Tool” in December 2025. The patent describes a device that latches to a vehicle doorframe striker and has an articulating leg attached to the engagement portion. A patent does not mean a product is ready for mass production or on store shelves. It protects the claimed invention and establishes intellectual property rights. It was a major milestone, but more work is needed to make the patented design a reliable product, including manufacturing, testing, regulatory considerations, supply chains and consumer input. It showed that the device had moved beyond a school project and into a formal innovation process. It also created a foundation for building a company around the technology.Meera did not build the company alone. She and her mother, Praveena Ramaswami, became co-founders of Cargility in 2025. Meera continued developing the technical solution, while Praveena left her career to focus full time on the business.The partnership combines engineering and commercial development. Meera understands the design and the problem that inspired it. Praveena has focused on evaluating the mobility ecosystem, building relationships and determining how the company can move toward manufacturing and customers. Starting a company for a physical product is not just having an invention. Founders need to find users, understand the healthcare and mobility market, figure out a pricing model, and decide how the device will be distributed. They must also test the product with the people it is meant to help.The mother daughter structure gives Cargility a personal connection to its mission. The company exists because a family experienced the emotional consequences of a fall and decided to look for a better way.Cargility is aimed at people who may need additional stability during vehicle transfers. That includes older adults, people recovering from rehabilitation and caregivers who help family members get in and out of cars.Vehicle transfers are often overlooked in discussions about accessibility. Public buildings may have ramps and lifts, but the journey begins at home and frequently includes the space between a car seat and the ground. A person may be able to walk once standing but still struggle with the transition.A portable device could be useful for people who travel in different vehicles or do not want permanent equipment installed. It may also help caregivers avoid lifting or pulling, reducing strain on both people.The product’s success will depend on real world testing and user trust. People need confidence that a device will remain secure, work on their vehicle and support them when balance is uncertain.Cargility is part of Ann Arbor’s expanding technology and entrepreneurship ecosystem. The city has programmes that connect founders with mentors, accelerators, university resources and funding opportunities. Ann Arbor SPARK has supported founders through initiatives including Entrepreneur Boot Camp, startup acceleration and other business programmes.For Cargility, that ecosystem can help bridge the gap between invention and commercial launch. Product development may require industrial designers, manufacturing partners, safety experts and investors. Local programmes can connect a small founding team with people who have experience in each area.The company has advanced to a working prototype with design for manufacturing completed and has been targeting an initial small production run and market launch. That stage is important because the best prototype is not always the easiest product to manufacture consistently. A design for manufacturing review helps identify ways to reduce complexity, control cost and maintain quality.Meera’s story began with a private family moment, but the problem she identified is widely shared. Falls can change how older adults and people with mobility limitations view daily activities. Fear can lead to fewer outings, less social contact and greater dependence on others.The Cargility device cannot remove every risk associated with movement. It can, however, address one vulnerable transition with a practical support. The invention shows how innovation often begins when someone pays close attention to an ordinary problem that others have accepted as unavoidable.Its future will depend on continued testing, responsible manufacturing and feedback from users. But the path from grandmother’s fall to patent and company already demonstrates the power of human centred design.Meera did not begin with the intention of becoming a founder. She began by wanting to make one moment safer for someone she loved. That empathy became an engineering question, the question became a prototype and the prototype became Cargility, an Ann Arbor company working to help people move with greater confidence and independence.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.
Article Summary: Cargility is a door to floor mobility assistive device. It engages with the striker in a vehicle’s doorframe and creates a stable support point. An articulating leg allows the user to lean on a railing while entering or exiting the vehicle. The design is intended to reduce fall risk and ease the physical strain placed on caregivers.
